{"tier": "statistical_data", "verdict": "not supported", "confidence": "high", "evidence": [{"claim_snippet": "93% of all human communication is nonverbal", "source_url": "https://www.spring.org.uk/2023/02/what-percentage-communication-nonverbal.php", "note": "States plainly that '93 percent of communication is nonverbal' is \"a myth deriving from studies by Albert Mehrabian.\""}, {"claim_snippet": "Research by Albert Mehrabian showed... all human communication", "source_url": "https://drnovak.medium.com/killing-the-myth-that-93-of-communication-is-nonverbal-9603e5e6f939", "note": "Notes Mehrabian's study used only 137 college undergraduates in narrow lab tasks judging single spoken words, not a study of 'all communication'."}, {"claim_snippet": "93% is nonverbal", "source_url": "https://law.temple.edu/aer/2021/05/03/brain-lessons-the-seven-percent-delusion/", "note": "Explains the 7/38/55 breakdown applies only to experiments about communicating feelings/attitudes (like-dislike), not general communication; the equations 'are not applicable' otherwise."}, {"claim_snippet": "93% of all human communication is nonverbal", "source_url": "https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Mehrabian", "note": "Describes the finding as the '7%-38%-55% Rule' concerning conveying feelings and attitudes, i.e., 93% nonverbal (38+55) only in that narrow context, not all communication."}, {"claim_snippet": "93% of all human communication is nonverbal", "source_url": "https://www.researchgate.net/publication/337463120_An_Urban_Legend_Called_The_73855_Ratio_Rule", "note": "Titled 'An Urban Legend Called The 7/38/55 Ratio Rule,' confirming the popularized generalization is a distortion of Mehrabian's narrower findings."}], "origin_trace": "Original source: Albert Mehrabian's 1967 studies (with M. Wiener and S. Ferris) on communication of feelings and attitudes, which produced the '7%-38%-55%' formula (words/tone/face) based on small experiments with ~137 undergraduates judging single ambiguous words and tone. This got popularized and generalized over decades into the sweeping claim that '93% of all communication is nonverbal,' a generalization Mehrabian himself and numerous researchers have explicitly rejected as a misapplication of his work.", "reasoning": "The 93% figure (7%+38%+55%-7%) does trace back to real numbers Mehrabian published, so the figure itself is not fabricated, but the claim massively distorts the scope and conditions: Mehrabian's data applied only to narrow lab experiments about judging a speaker's feelings/attitudes from single spoken words and tone, with a small non-representative sample, not to 'all human communication' in general (e.g., factual, informational, or written communication). Mehrabian himself and multiple independent analyses call the generalized '93% nonverbal' claim a myth/urban legend, explicitly stating the ratio is inapplicable outside the emotion-judgment context it was derived from. Because the numeric figure is genuine but the framing (population, scope, and universality) is badly distorted, this is a mixed/oversold statistic, but given the near-universal debunking by sources including the original research context, it is best classified as not supported as stated."}

{"tier": "statistical_data", "verdict": "not supported", "confidence": "high", "evidence": [{"claim_snippet": "women speak about 20,000 words a day while men speak only about 7,000", "source_url": "https://www.npr.org/2007/07/05/11762186/study-men-talk-just-as-much-as-women", "note": "2007 Science study by Mehl et al. found women speak ~16,215 words/day and men ~15,669, with the difference \"not statistically significant\" \u2014 directly contradicting the 20,000 vs 7,000 figures."}, {"claim_snippet": "A study found that women speak about 20,000 words a day", "source_url": "https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/women-talk-more-than-men/", "note": "Traces the 20,000/7,000 figures to Louann Brizendine's 2006 book The Female Brain, not a scientific study; the article states the new Science study reports men and women \"actually use roughly the same number of words daily.\""}, {"claim_snippet": "men speak only about 7,000", "source_url": "https://languagelog.ldc.upenn.edu/nll/?p=4488", "note": "Language Log documents the 20,000/7,000 figures being uncritically repeated by media (ABC, USA Today, CBS) citing Brizendine, without any traceable original study."}, {"claim_snippet": "A study found that women speak about 20,000 words a day while men speak only about 7,000", "source_url": "https://medium.com/no-time/do-women-really-speak-more-than-men-debunking-the-viral-word-count-myth-0a7192f0bdab", "note": "Reports that Brizendine 'didn\u2019t cite a credible scientific source for that claim' and the number was later removed from newer editions of her book after academic criticism."}, {"claim_snippet": "women speak about 20,000 words a day", "source_url": "https://www.jpost.com/science/science-around-the-world/article-840587", "note": "More recent research (post-2007) found women speak ~13,349 and men ~11,950 words/day, again far from the 20,000/7,000 figures, and explicitly states the Brizendine figures were 'not supported by reliable scientific evidence.'"}], "origin_trace": "Earliest traceable origin is Louann Brizendine's 2006 book 'The Female Brain,' which asserted women use ~20,000 words/day vs. men's ~7,000, without citing a scientific source; a University of Pennsylvania researcher who tried to trace it further found it may originate from an unsourced 1993 marriage-counseling pamphlet. No peer-reviewed study has ever produced these figures.", "reasoning": "The claim presents an unsourced, uncredited statistic as if it were the finding of 'a study,' but the actual peer-reviewed research (Mehl et al., 2007, Science) found men and women speak roughly the same number of words per day (~16,000 each, not statistically significant), and a more recent large-scale study found women ~13,349 vs men ~11,950 \u2014 both far from 20,000 vs 7,000. Multiple journalistic and academic sources trace the 20,000/7,000 figures to Brizendine's popular-science book rather than any actual study, and note the figures were later dropped due to lack of scientific backing. This is a clear case where the purported 'study' behind the claim does not exist as described, and actual studies contradict the figures."}
